newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedes more pessimistic about living standard - poll.
newsitem.headline: Swedes more pessimistic about living standard - poll.

text.p: Swedish households turned more pessimistic about their living standard, but slightly less pessimistic about the country's economy in December, according to a report on household expectations by pollster SKOP.
Three out of 10 Swedes believed in December that their living standard would decline in 1997 compared with 29 percent both in October and for all of 1996, SKOP said.
Expectations about living standards are the most important factor for private consumption, according to SKOP.

Households were, however, slightly less pessimistic about the country's economy, with nearly 44 percent believing it will worsen over one year, compared with 46 percent in October. Nearly 23 percent see the economy improving, against somewhat more than 19 percent in the earlier poll, SKOP said.
"After some months with significant buying interest for a string of capital goods, households in December show a clearly weaker interest, in some cases weaker than a year ago," SKOP said.
Expectations for inflation remained stable with 18 percent of households counting on higher inflation during 1997 and 12 percent a lower inflation.
Since February 1996, households maintain expectations for a small rise in prices.
In December, the number of households planning to buy a new car in the next three months fell to 3.4 percent from 4.9 percent in October.
Regarding savings, 21 percent of households said they would save more money in 1997, while 10 percent said they would save less.
